narrative:
The model estimates a 49% chance that you will leave your job, which is high enough for the company to deny your promotion as a precaution.

Three main factors shaped this outlook. First, your total years of experience across all jobs had the strongest influence and pulled the prediction toward staying. Most employees the model expects to stay have similar short-to-mid experience levels, so this worked in your favor. Second, having received other job offers while at the company was the next strongest driver and pushed the prediction toward leaving. The model sees this as a clear sign you have attractive outside options. Third, your feeling that you have already received the promotions you deserved worked to keep the prediction lower, though not enough to overcome the other signals.

Taken together, the combination of solid outside opportunities outweighed the protective effects of your experience and past promotion satisfaction, tipping the balance just enough for the system to flag a departure risk.

The organization should discuss your career goals openly and explore whether better internal growth paths could reduce the appeal of external offers. You may also want to reflect on what would make staying feel like the clearer choice. Addressing these points now could change the outlook for future decisions.
